By analyzing the recently proposed reward-augmented decoding approach (RAD), which uses a higher-rank expert model, we introduce a simpler but more efficient low-rank parametrization of the expert model enabling fast and effective guided decoding. We empirically show that the low-rank RAD performs on par with the more flexible RAD on a detoxification and a sentiment control task, while requiring only a single reward model call per generated token.
cross_field_papers.tldr: This work revisits an effective and modular approach for controllability of the language models, when an external expert model guides the decoding, and introduces a simpler but more efficient low-rank parametrization of the expert model enabling fast and effective guided decoding.

cross_field_papers.title: Controlled Language Generation for Language Learning Items
cross_field_papers.abstract: This work aims to employ natural language generation (NLG) to rapidly generate items for English language learning applications: this requires both language models capable of generating fluent, high-quality English, and to control the output of the generation to match the requirements of the relevant items. We experiment with deep pretrained models for this task, developing novel methods for controlling items for factors relevant in language learning: diverse sentences for different proficiency levels and argument structure to test grammar. Human evaluation demonstrates high grammatically scores for all models (3.4 and above out of 4), and higher length (24%) and complexity (9%) over the baseline for the advanced proficiency model. Our results show that we can achieve strong performance while adding additional control to ensure diverse, tailored content for individual users.
cross_field_papers.venue: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
cross_field_papers.tldr: The results show that this work can achieve strong performance while adding additional control to ensure diverse, tailored content for individual users, and develop novel methods for controlling items for factors relevant in language learning.

cross_field_papers.title: Context Matters in Semantically Controlled Language Generation for Task-oriented Dialogue Systems
cross_field_papers.abstract: This work combines information about the dialogue history encoded by pre-trained model with a meaning representation of the current system utterance to realise contextual language generation in task-oriented dialogues. We utilise the pre-trained multi-context ConveRT model for context representation in a model trained from scratch; and leverage the immediate preceding user utterance for context generation in a model adapted from the pre-trained GPT-2. Both experiments with the MultiWOZ dataset show that contextual information encoded by pre-trained model improves the performance of response generation both in automatic metrics and human evaluation. Our presented contextual generator enables higher variety of generated responses that fit better to the ongoing dialogue. Analysing the context size shows that longer context does not automatically lead to better performance, but the immediate preceding user utterance plays an essential role for contextual generation. In addition, we also propose a re-ranker for the GPT-based generation model. The experiments show that the response selected by the re-ranker has a significant improvement on automatic metrics.
cross_field_papers.tldr: This work combines information about the dialogue history encoded by pre-trained model with a meaning representation of the current system utterance to realise contextual language generation in task-oriented dialogues and proposes a re-ranker for the GPT-based generation model.

cross_field_papers.title: Fast Controlled Generation from Language Models with Adaptive Weighted Rejection Sampling
cross_field_papers.abstract: The dominant approach to generating from language models subject to some constraint is locally constrained decoding (LCD), incrementally sampling tokens at each time step such that the constraint is never violated. Typically, this is achieved through token masking: looping over the vocabulary and excluding non-conforming tokens. There are two important problems with this approach. (i) Evaluating the constraint on every token can be prohibitively expensive -- LM vocabularies often exceed $100,000$ tokens. (ii) LCD can distort the global distribution over strings, sampling tokens based only on local information, even if they lead down dead-end paths. This work introduces a new algorithm that addresses both these problems. First, to avoid evaluating a constraint on the full vocabulary at each step of generation, we propose an adaptive rejection sampling algorithm that typically requires orders of magnitude fewer constraint evaluations. Second, we show how this algorithm can be extended to produce low-variance, unbiased estimates of importance weights at a very small additional cost -- estimates that can be soundly used within previously proposed sequential Monte Carlo algorithms to correct for the myopic behavior of local constraint enforcement. Through extensive empirical evaluation in text-to-SQL, molecular synthesis, goal inference, pattern matching, and JSON domains, we show that our approach is superior to state-of-the-art baselines, supporting a broader class of constraints and improving both runtime and performance. Additional theoretical and empirical analyses show that our method's runtime efficiency is driven by its dynamic use of computation, scaling with the divergence between the unconstrained and constrained LM, and as a consequence, runtime improvements are greater for better models.
cross_field_papers.tldr: This work proposes an adaptive rejection sampling algorithm that typically requires orders of magnitude fewer constraint evaluations, and shows how this algorithm can be extended to produce low-variance, unbiased estimates of importance weights at a very small additional cost.

cross_field_papers.title: Controlled generation in example-based machine translation
cross_field_papers.abstract:
The theme of controlled translation is currently in vogue in the area of MT. Recent research (Sch¨aler et al., 2003;

Carl, 2003) hypothesises that EBMT systems are perhaps best suited to this challenging task. In this paper, we present

an EBMT system where the generation of the target string is filtered by data written according to controlled language

specifications. As far as we are aware, this is the only research available on this topic. In the field of controlled language applications, it is more usual to constrain the source language in this way rather than the target. We translate a small corpus of controlled English into French using the on-line MT system Logomedia, and seed the memories of our EBMT system with a set of automatically induced lexical resources using the Marker Hypothesis as a segmentation tool. We test our system on a large set of sentences extracted from a Sun Translation Memory, and provide both an automatic and a human evaluation. For comparative purposes, we also provide results for Logomedia itself

cross_field_papers.title: Example-based controlled translation
cross_field_papers.abstract:
The first research on integrating controlled language data in an Example-Based Machine Translation (EBMT) system was published in [Gough & Way, 2003]. We improve on their sub-sentential alignment algorithm to populate the system’s databases with more than six times as many potentially useful fragments. Together with two simple novel improvements—correcting mistranslations in the lexicon, and allowing multiple translations in the lexicon—translation quality improves considerably when target language

translations are constrained. We also develop the first EBMT system which attempts to filter the source language data using controlled language specifications. We provide

detailed automatic and human evaluations of a number of experiments carried out to test the quality of the system. We observe that our system outperforms Logomedia in a number of tests. Finally, despite conflicting results from different automatic evaluation metrics, we observe a preference for controlling the source data rather than the target translations

fields_explored.rationale: Several papers discuss readability and its impact on comprehension, particularly for specific audiences like learners with reading difficulties or non-experts in biomedical fields [144f70267c3bc8d76e8e91d267f6921cadcc4e29, 333002756, 44f02e037fd78116f921c8c57bc9ee3f7b2e64fd]. Cognitive psychology offers theories and methods for measuring readability and understanding how text complexity affects comprehension, which could inform how to quantify and optimize readability in extractive summarization.

Research on perceived text quality and readability in summaries [d7bbf98163850b8c54b0637d7400f55b37ab29b9] and studies on how compression rate affects readability [fe833639b6f7b68c00cd1a53264fc2af47a60922] align with HCI’s interest in user experience and usability. HCI provides frameworks for evaluating how users interact with and judge the quality of generated content, which can guide the development of summarization systems that prioritize both factual accuracy and readability.

The need for controlled language and readability in summarization [333002756, 4763720] and the use of readability measures [340262610] points to computational linguistics, which focuses on formal models of language processing and generation. Methods from computational linguistics—such as syntactic parsing, lexical analysis, and readability scoring algorithms—could enhance extractive summarization systems to better balance factual accuracy and readability.

bridge_insights.insight: Readability measures that focus on syntactic complexity and lexical features, such as those used in controlled language approaches, can be adapted to evaluate and control the readability of extractive summaries to improve factual accuracy by reducing cognitive load on readers.
bridge_insights.connection_to_core_problem: Since the core problem concerns how readability affects factual accuracy in extractive summarization, applying cognitive psychology's readability metrics can help quantify and manage the readability of summaries, potentially reducing misinterpretations that lead to factual errors.

bridge_insights.insight: Eye-tracking and gaze behavior studies in cognitive psychology show that increased cognitive load correlates with difficulty in comprehension, suggesting that extractive summarization systems could benefit from incorporating gaze-informed metrics to optimize readability and thus reduce factual inaccuracies.
bridge_insights.connection_to_core_problem: If readability impacts comprehension and cognitive load, then monitoring gaze behavior during reading of summaries can inform how to adjust summarization strategies to maintain clarity and accuracy.

bridge_insights.insight: Sentence splitting and simplification techniques from cognitive psychology research can guide extractive summarization algorithms to avoid overly complex sentence structures that impair comprehension, thereby supporting more accurate factual representation.
bridge_insights.connection_to_core_problem: Extractive summarization systems that preserve readability by avoiding overly complex sentence structures may reduce the likelihood of misinterpretation and improve factual consistency.

bridge_insights.insight: Studies showing that text format and font readability affect reading comprehension in children and adults suggest that extractive summarization systems should consider formatting and layout factors to improve readability and reduce factual misinterpretation.
bridge_insights.connection_to_core_problem: Improving the readability of extractive summaries through formatting considerations aligns with cognitive psychology findings that readability affects comprehension, which in turn influences the perceived accuracy of the summary.

bridge_insights.insight: Human-centered readability evaluation frameworks from human-computer interaction emphasize the importance of clarity, tone, and trustworthiness in text, which can be integrated into extractive summarization to ensure that summaries are not only readable but also factually trustworthy.
bridge_insights.connection_to_core_problem: By incorporating human-centered readability criteria, extractive summarization systems can be guided toward producing summaries that are both easy to read and factually accurate, addressing the core concern of readability affecting factual accuracy.

research_question: How does the readability of a source document affect the factual accuracy of extractive summarisation of it?
